passage:
At the bus stop in the village, while the whole group waited for the late bus, Sachin cracked a joke about Binita's mother's old scooter, making a "putt-putt" noise and wobbling like a rider. The others giggled. Binita's face went still. "That one's not okay," Binita said, in a calm voice, looking straight at Sachin. "Please don't joke about my mother."
Sachin stopped, mouth open. "Oh. Sorry, I didn't think."
"Thanks." Binita smiled a small smile. "Ask me about the goat kids instead. There are two new ones."
"Really? Show me later," said Sachin, and the moment eased. When the bus finally came, they sat together and talked about the goats all the way to the market town.

qa.q: What did Sachin joke about?
qa.a: Binita's mother's old scooter.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the face went still?
qa.a: Hurt and serious. Binita did not want joking about the mother and chose to say so.

qa.q: What worked about the way Binita said stop?
qa.a: Binita said it once, clearly and calmly, named the boundary, and then offered a friendly change of subject.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel after being told "That one's not okay"?
qa.a: Surprised and a little embarrassed, but ready to adjust, since Sachin apologised and asked to see the goat kids.

grounding: A teenager calmly says that one is not okay and offers a new topic, and Sachin adjusts.

passage:
In the courtyard of the school in Lisbon, Astrid was laughing about the pictures from the trip. "And Beatriz, in that photo you looked like a surprised fish!" The others joined in. Beatriz smiled tightly. The first time, it was funny. The fifth time, it wasn't. "Hey, did you all finish the maths sheet?" Beatriz asked, changing the subject. Astrid held up the phone again. Beatriz put a hand out gently. "Astrid, I'd like you to stop with that photo. I'm not okay with it."
"Oh," said Astrid, and put the phone away. "Sure. Sorry."
"Thanks," said Beatriz. "Now, the maths sheet?"

qa.q: Where did the conversation happen?
qa.a: In the courtyard of the school in Lisbon.

qa.q: What did Beatriz feel about the photo joke by the fifth time?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and annoyed. The joke was funny once, but not repeated, and Beatriz's smile was tight.

qa.q: What did Beatriz do first, and what did Beatriz do when that did not work?
qa.a: Beatriz first changed the subject to the maths sheet, and when Astrid raised the photo again, said clearly, "I'd like you to stop with that photo. I'm not okay with it."

qa.q: How might Astrid feel after Beatriz says stop?
qa.a: A bit surprised, but accepting, since Astrid put the phone away, apologised and moved on to the maths sheet.

grounding: A teenager first changes the subject and then names the boundary once and clearly, and Astrid adjusts.

passage: In the school library, Sahil leaned over Minakshi's shoulder. "Your dad drives a bus, right? So you'll get free rides to college, lucky!" A few kids laughed. Minakshi looked up. She didn't laugh. She said calmly, "That one's not okay, Sahil. My dad works hard." Sahil blinked. "I was just joking." "I know. That one's not funny to me." There was a pause. Then Sahil said, "Okay. Sorry." Minakshi nodded and went back to her book. The next day Sahil sat next to her in class and asked about the history homework like nothing had happened. He never mentioned her father's job again.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's father do?
qa.a: He drives a bus.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when Sahil made the joke?
qa.a: She felt hurt and protective of her father, but stayed calm.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's calm 'That one's not okay' work?
qa.a: It named the boundary once, clearly, without anger, so Sahil could adjust instead of getting defensive.

qa.q: How did Sahil respond to Minakshi's boundary?
qa.a: He apologised and never mentioned her father's job again, showing he respected it.

grounding: Shows a teenager naming a boundary calmly and clearly once, and a friend adjusting.

passage:
Dear Neel,

You asked how I stopped Abhinav's jokes about my stammer. I'll tell you exactly.

For months, whenever I got stuck on a word, Abhinav would copy it: "K-k-k-Kunal!" Everyone laughed, and I laughed too, because I didn't want to seem touchy.

Last week, in the canteen, he did it again. I put my sandwich down and said, as calmly as I could, "Abhinav, that one's not okay. Please stop." My heart was pounding.

He looked surprised. Then he said, "Oh. Sorry, man, I didn't know it bothered you." And he stopped. Just like that.

He's still my friend. He's actually been nicer since.

So say it once, clearly. Good friends change.

Kunal

qa.q: What did Abhinav copy?
qa.a: Kunal's stammer.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when saying 'that one's not okay'?
qa.a: Kunal felt nervous, heart pounding, but determined to set the boundary.

qa.q: What made Kunal's boundary work?
qa.a: Saying it once, calmly and clearly, instead of laughing along, which let Abhinav understand and adjust.

qa.q: How did Abhinav respond?
qa.a: He was surprised, apologised, and stopped, and has been nicer since.

grounding: Shows a teenager naming a boundary calmly and clearly once, and a friend adjusting.

passage:
"Anjali, you remember when you kept joking about my mum's accent? Okay, don't make that face, I'm not angry anymore. I'm Arohi, and I want to tell you why I said something.
At first I laughed with you. But every time, I felt a little knot in my stomach. My mum learned English at thirty. She's proud of it.
So that day at the bus stop, when you did the voice again, I just said, 'That one's not okay for me. Can we not?' And I changed the subject to the cricket match.
You went quiet. Then you said, 'Oh. Sorry, I didn't think.' And you never did it again.
I'm telling you because it worked. I'd been scared you'd call me dramatic. But you didn't. You just adjusted. That's how I knew you were a good friend."

qa.q: At what age did Arohi's mum learn English?
qa.a: At thirty.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling each time Anjali joked?
qa.a: Arohi felt a little knot in the stomach, hurt on behalf of a mum who is proud of her English.

qa.q: What made Arohi's approach effective?
qa.a: Saying calmly, once, 'That one's not okay for me' and then changing the subject, which let Anjali adjust without a fight.

qa.q: How did Anjali respond when Arohi said stop?
qa.a: Anjali went quiet, apologised, and never did it again.

grounding: Shows a teenager naming a boundary calmly once and changing the subject, and a friend adjusting.

passage: I sat one table behind them in the canteen, so I heard all of it. Santosh was on a roll with jokes about everyone's parents. Then he started on Bhavna's mother, who sells vegetables at the Tuesday market, something about her "business empire". The table laughed. Bhavna didn't. She put her spoon down and said, in a completely normal voice, "That one's not okay. Pick another topic." No shouting, no laughing it off. For a second it went quiet. I thought Santosh would push back. Instead he rubbed his neck and said, "Fair. Sorry." Then he asked her about the maths test. I couldn't tell what she felt inside; her face stayed calm. But the next week, I noticed, the jokes about parents had stopped.

qa.q: What does Bhavna's mother sell?
qa.a: She sells vegetables at the Tuesday market.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been feeling when she put her spoon down?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and angry about the joke, yet she seemed steady and confident enough to name the limit calmly.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna's words work better than laughing it off?
qa.a: She named the limit once, clearly and calmly, so there was no confusion and Santosh could adjust without a fight.

qa.q: How did Santosh respond to the boundary?
qa.a: He seemed a little embarrassed, rubbed his neck, said "Fair. Sorry," and changed the subject, adjusting the way a good friend would.

grounding: Seen by a classmate, a teenager calmly says a joke about her mother is not okay, and her friend adjusts.
